Research topic

Supply Chain Visibility with Large Language Models

Building an auditable map of inter-firm supplier-customer relationships in China by combining large language models, web-scale information retrieval, and network science.

Updated 2026-09-17 · Keywords: supply chain, large language models, knowledge graph, OSINT, network science, China

What I did

I develop Supply Chain OSINT Agent, a research pipeline that discovers supplier-customer relationships between firms from public web evidence and assembles them into a supply chain knowledge graph (SCKG), where firms are nodes and inter-firm transactions are edges. The work is carried out by Hiroto Fukada as a PhD student in Informatics at SOKENDAI (The Graduate University for Advanced Studies) and a Research Assistant at the National Institute of Informatics (NII), together with Takayuki Mizuno.

The distinguishing choice is the unit of evidence. Instead of crawling and processing full web pages, the pipeline treats web search snippets - the short, query-biased summaries returned alongside search results - as a first-pass evidence layer for LLM-based relationship extraction. Every extracted edge retains its provenance metadata, so each relationship can be traced back to the text that produced it and audited later.

Why it matters

In China, supplier-customer disclosure is typically limited to the major partners of listed firms. Unlisted firms and long-tail inter-firm links are poorly captured in structured data, which means official statistics and commercial databases share the same blind spots. Anyone reasoning about economic security, export controls, or the industrial interdependence between China and Taiwan is reasoning from a partial map.

Full-text web mining could fill that gap in principle, but not at scale: pages are often inaccessible or expensive to process, and feeding them to large language models consumes orders of magnitude more tokens than the additional information justifies. The practical question is therefore not whether LLMs can read the web, but which unit of evidence makes web-scale extraction affordable and auditable at the same time.

Approach

Snippet-driven extraction. Search snippets are used as a scalable first pass for LLM-based relationship extraction, with full-text processing reserved for the candidates that need confirmation. This keeps token cost proportional to the evidence actually used.

Prompt optimization. The extraction prompts are optimized rather than hand-tuned, which matters for disambiguating firm names and for deciding the direction of a relationship - which side supplies which - from a short, context-poor snippet. This part of the pipeline was presented at JSAI 2026.

Network science. Once the graph exists, its structure is analysed with tools from network science: bow-tie decomposition of the inter-firm transaction network, degree distributions, and interdependence measures between industries and regions. This is where a knowledge graph becomes a statement about resilience rather than a list of edges, and it is the focus of the NetSci 2026 and NetEco 2026 presentations.

Results

The IEEE CIFEr 2026 paper evaluates the pipeline on 130,685 Chinese firms used as search seeds, covering Shanghai- and Shenzhen-listed firms and large unlisted firms as of 2024. On the listed-firm subset, the resulting supply chain knowledge graph covers 7.2 times more firms and 9.3 times more relationships than the CSMAR disclosure-based benchmark, and reveals heavy-tailed degree patterns that disclosure data alone does not show.

The cost trade-off is stated explicitly rather than hidden. Exhaustive full-text chunking discovers 19.8 times more unique relationships than snippets, but requires 251.2 times more input tokens and yields higher redundancy. Snippets are therefore positioned as a scalable first-pass evidence layer and an auditable complement to disclosure-based databases, not as a replacement for full-text reading.

Results have been presented at IEEE CIFEr 2026 (accepted paper), NetSci 2026, JSAI 2026, and the Network Ecology Symposium, where the study received a Best Poster Award at NetEco 2026.
